summary: An excerpt from a fiction book (Book 1, part 133) in which a teenage hacker known as M1k3y, a character in a story about a movement called Xnet, answers questions from journalists after a San Francisco attack. M1k3y argues that the DHS is failing to keep people safe, that its surveillance and suspicion tactics terrify citizens the way terrorism does, and that the teen's own hacking skills show terrorists could easily do the same things. The passage ends with M1k3y handing the keyboard to Ange and with Marcus's personal troubles introduced.
one_line: Fiction excerpt where teen hacker M1k3y answers journalists' questions about DHS failures, surveillance, and terrorism after a San Francisco bridge attack.
key_facts: M1k3y is a 17-year-old who says they figured out how to make an Internet that the government cannot wiretap.
M1k3y says they figured out how to jam the DHS's person-tracking technology.
M1k3y claims they could turn innocent people into suspects and guilty people into innocents in the government's eyes.
M1k3y says they could get metal onto an airplane or beat a no-fly list.
Doug Christensen is identified as a reporter from the Washington Internet Daily.
M1k3y states that the DHS would not stop the bridge from being blown up again, and that its tracing, loss of freedom, and turning citizens against each other fail to make the city safer.
M1k3y says: "The point of terrorism is to terrify us. The DHS terrifies me."
M1k3y says: "if this is a free country then I should be able to at least say what my own cops do to me."
A journalist from the Sydney Morning Herald questions M1k3y during the press exchange.
Some people in the discussion say terrorists and the government are either literally the same or equally bad.
Some people say the government knows how to catch terrorists but prefers not to because "war presidents" get re-elected.
M1k3y says "If I can do it, terrorists can do it."
M1k3y hands the keyboard to Ange so she can be M1k3y for a while.
M1k3y reflects that M1k3y was the kind of kid who talked to international journalists and inspired a movement.
Marcus got suspended from school, fought with his dad, and wondered about his own situation at the end of the excerpt.
